title: Ezekiel 20:1–9
context: Ezekiel, the prophet, narrates that in the seventh year (counted, as elsewhere in the book, from King Jehoiachin’s exile; compare 1:2; 8:1), some elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD and sat before him, as in 14:1. The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel, whom he addresses as son of man, the usual title for the prophet in this book (compare 2:1). The LORD refuses to be inquired of by these elders and instead tells Ezekiel to make them know the abominations of their fathers. He then begins a review of Israel’s history: in Egypt he chose Israel, swore to bring them out to a good land, and commanded them to throw away the idols of Egypt, but they rebelled. He resolved to pour out his wrath, yet he acted for his name’s sake, so that his name would not be profaned among the nations who had seen him make himself known (compare Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13; Psalm 106:8). The phrase for my name’s sake recurs through the chapter. Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat it as shared ground: God’s faithfulness to his own name and purpose stands behind his mercy to a rebellious people.

verses.text: In the seventh year, in the fifth month, the tenth day of the month, some of the elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD, and sat before me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezekiel dating the visit of the elders who came to inquire of the LORD and sat before him. They seek a word from God in exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the setting carefully dated within Jehoiachin’s exile (compare 1:2). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for a searching answer to the elders.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Ezekiel. The prophet speaks only what he receives from God, not his own opinions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophetic word coming from God, not the prophet’s own mind. Both traditions commonly read the verse as underscoring the divine source of the message that follows.

verses.text: “Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Is it to inquire of me that you have come? As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “I will not be inquired of by you.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD, addressing Ezekiel as son of man, refusing to be inquired of by the elders. Their inquiry is not sincere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God refusing those who cling to idols (compare 14:3). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against seeking God while holding on to sin.

verses.text: “Will you judge them, son of man? Will you judge them? Cause them to know the abominations of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel to judge the elders by making known their fathers’ abominations. History becomes a mirror.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet called to expose a long pattern of sin. Both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing an honest review of Israel’s past.

verses.text: Tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “In the day when I chose Israel, and swore to the offspring of the house of Jacob, and made myself known to them in the land of Egypt, when I swore to them, saying, ‘I am the LORD your God;’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD recalling the day he chose Israel and made himself known in Egypt. His choice was gracious and covenantal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign choice of Israel and his self-revelation (compare Exodus 6:7). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as grounding the history in God’s initiative.

verses.text: in that day I swore to them to bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had searched out for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD swearing to bring Israel to a land he had searched out, flowing with milk and honey. God’s promise was generous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to his oath (compare Exodus 3:8). Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing the goodness of God’s purpose for his people.

verses.text: I said to them, ‘Each of you throw away the abominations of his eyes. Don’t defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD commanding Israel to throw away the idols of Egypt. Covenant loyalty required turning from false gods.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s call to exclusive worship from the very beginning. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about the demand to forsake idols.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But they rebelled against me and wouldn’t listen to me. They didn’t all throw away the abominations of their eyes. They also didn’t forsake the idols of Egypt. Then I said I would pour out my wrath on them, to accomplish my anger against them in the middle of the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel rebelling, refusing to listen, and clinging to Egypt’s idols, so that the LORD resolved to pour out his wrath. Their rebellion was real and culpable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the depth of Israel’s sin even in Egypt. Both traditions commonly read the verse as an honest account that does not idealize Israel’s past.

verses.text: But I worked for my name’s sake, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations among which they were, in whose sight I made myself known to them in bringing them out of the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD acting for his name’s sake so it would not be profaned among the nations. God’s concern for his name led to mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s glory as the ground of his saving action (compare Psalm 106:8; Isaiah 48:9). Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s purpose in history.
